Pylate stood before the crowd with two prisoners.
And in some ancient copies of Matthew, both men were named Jesus.
Which one do you want?
Matthew, chapter twenty seven.
It is Passover in Jerusalem. Jesus has been arrested, and handed to the Roman governor, Pontius Pylate.
At the feast, the governor would release one prisoner. Whomever the people wanted.
And they had a notable prisoner. Barabbas.
Mark says he lay bound with the rebels, who had committed murder in the insurrection.
So Pylate asks: Whom will ye that I release unto you? Barabbas, or Jesus, which is called Christ?
Then a message arrives. From his own wife.
Have thou nothing to do with that just man. I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.
But the chief priests work the crowd.
Which of the two? And the crowd shouts one name.
Barabbas!
What then shall I do with Jesus? Let him be crucified.
Pylate washes his hands. I am innocent of the blood of this just person.
Barabbas walks out free. Jesus is led away to the cross.
But here is the part most people never hear.
Around the year two fifty, the scholar Orijen wrote that copies of Matthew in his day called him, Jesus Barabbas.
He suspected the name was dropped, so a sinner would not carry the name of Jesus.
Some ancient manuscripts still have it. Several modern Bibles now print it.
And Barabbas means, in Aramaic, son of the father.
So Pylate's choice was this.
Jesus, son of the father. Or Jesus, the Son of the Father.
The guilty one walked free. The innocent one died in his place.
Barabbas was the first man who could say it, word for word. Jesus took my place.
